stories.topic: From Aurangzeb to a knife at King John's throat
stories.summary: Ajay traces how humanity learned to shrink the king. Under monarchy, the ruler's word was total: Aurangzeb could order a beheading, and the Pope crowned Napoleon to bless absolute authority. Rome ran the first experiment with a republic, where about fifty families took power from the monarch and set up judges, until it was 'destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar.' The story restarted in England in 1215. King John was demanding crazy taxes and loans, so a group of merchants and finance people seized him, put a knife to his throat and forced him to sign the Magna Carta. Its language looks archaic and flimsy today, but it was the first clear statement that a king's power has limits. That journey ran through Parliament to Cromwell and the beheading of Charles I. It then reached Montesquieu's proposal to cut the state into three pieces, and finally Articles 1, 2 and 3 of the US Constitution.
stories.insight: Limits on power were not gifted by rulers. They were extracted, and each step built on people watching the previous one work. Separation of powers is the mature form of a centuries-old project to make sure no one has a king's authority.
stories.quote: they put a knife to his throat and they forced him to sign

stories.summary: In the Constituent Assembly, Professor K.T. Shah moved a resolution, Article 40A, to write a clear separation of powers into the Constitution. Ajay reads Ambedkar's reply. Ambedkar accepted that the executive must be separate from the judiciary. He argued against separating the executive from the legislature as the US does, saying many Americans disliked that rigidity. He also said Parliament's work was so vast and complicated that MPs needed direct guidance from executive members sitting in Parliament. So India began with no meaningful separation of powers. Amit adds that the choice should be judged in its context: the country was falling apart and today's map did not yet exist. The point is to learn from it, not to judge personalities.
stories.insight: India's executive-heavy state was not an accident. Its most respected framer chose it deliberately and gave reasons. It shows how a reasonable-sounding design choice can shape a country for decades.
stories.quote: I personally therefore do not think that there is any very great loss that is likely to occur if we do not adopt the American method of separating the executive from the legislature.

stories.topic: Nehru, Shastri and the Babri idol
stories.summary: When the Ram idol was placed inside the Babri Masjid, Nehru in Delhi ordered it removed within a couple of days, before things got out of hand. But the UP chief minister was Govind Ballabh Pant and his deputy was Lal Bahadur Shastri. Shastri, who would have had to carry out the order, refused. Amit wishes that in this case they had obeyed Nehru. His broader point is that the Congress of the 1950s and 60s was a 'grand tent': local politicians could defy the centre, and the local party chose its own chief minister. In the 1970s Indira Gandhi centralised power, and the high command began appointing chief ministers.
stories.insight: Democracy inside a party is itself a check on power. When it disappeared and the anti-defection law came in, a ruling party could control both the executive and the legislature from the top.
stories.quote: Before this you couldn't freaking appoint a chief minister, the local party would decide it, the things would flow from the bottom up to some extent.

stories.topic: Standing committees: a great institution that lived only in norms
stories.summary: People saw that a joint secretary writing the laws was a farce. So, starting with Shivraj Patil, a norm grew of sending important bills to parliamentary standing committees. When Ajay was in the Ministry of Finance, the Speaker would refer a bill to a committee if it drew significant criticism. The committees had both ruling and opposition MPs and were chaired by opposition members. They debated the bill, summoned expert witnesses and questioned the civil servants who drafted it. Ajay appeared before many as an expert. He counts this among the good things behind India's 1991–2011 growth episode. But it was never written into the rules, and today, he says, there is really no check and balance around these things.
stories.insight: This is the core lesson of public choice theory. A check that exists only as a custom can vanish quietly. If it isn't written into law or the Constitution, it isn't real.
stories.quote: I've had the privilege of being an expert with many, many standing committees. It was fabulous. It was a great institution. Unfortunately, it was only in norms.

stories.topic: SEBI: where the judge, prosecutor and investigator have lunch together
stories.summary: SEBI was created in 1992 by founders Ajay deeply respects, including Surendra Dave and Ravi Narain. It copied practices from RBI and ended up with all three branches of the state under one roof. It drafts regulations, which are laws written by unelected officials; Ajay says the original Act had 'excessive delegation.' It investigates and prosecutes, with those two roles mixed up. And a SEBI employee plays judge while a colleague prosecutes. Appeals originally went to the Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), who sat on SEBI's board. Early orders simply declared someone guilty and imposed a fine of, say, ₹10 crore, with no reasoning at all. Other countries do it differently. At the US SEC, the administrative law judge sits in a courtroom inside the building but belongs to the judiciary. In Britain's FCA model and Australia's twin-peaks model, the regulator builds a case and takes it to a court or tribunal. Ajay reckons India is about 30% of the way to fixing this.
stories.insight: Without separation of powers, a regulator quietly becomes a miniature state. The clean model is that the regulator stops at investigating and deciding whether to prosecute, and then hands the case to a real judge.
stories.quote: And the judge and the prosecutor and the investigator go have lunch together

stories.topic: The 1992 bet against the Bombay High Court
stories.summary: SEBI's founders put a judge inside the regulator because, in 1992, they thought the Bombay High Court was so bad that nothing would ever get done. Ajay cites recent quantitative work from XKDR Forum. It shows the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and efficient, and improving. The gap between adjudication at SEBI and at these courts is no longer large.
stories.insight: Every institutional design reflects the constraints of its time. When those constraints change, the trade-offs should be re-examined rather than kept by default.
stories.quote: And it is not fair to have a sweeping rejection of the speed and the intellectual power of these courts today.

stories.topic: America pushes back on its administrative state
stories.summary: Under Roosevelt, the US federal government built agency upon agency. Nervous Republicans pushed through the Administrative Procedure Act in 1946. Later, court orders in a case involving the oil company Chevron created 'Chevron deference.' Under it, if an agency expert had applied her mind and drafted a regulation, judges could review only the process, not the substance. Many saw this as letting legislative power seep into the administrative state. In 2024 the US Supreme Court largely struck it down. In a second development, someone argued that the SEC's in-house administrative law judge denied him his constitutional right to a jury trial. The Supreme Court struck down that SEC arrangement as unconstitutional. Ajay calls the field 'red hot', and the Emerging Markets Conference held a whole session on it.
stories.insight: Even the model constitutional democracy has to keep fighting against power drifting to unelected officials. Settled arrangements can be reopened, and they can move in a good direction.
stories.quote: You may be the best expert in the world, you may have 15 PhDs, but a judge can reopen a matter and question what the regulation is

recommendations.creator: David Friedman
recommendations.context: Ajay borrowed Friedman's phrase 'the machinery of freedom' for the practical machinery of liberty: decentralisation, separation of powers, keeping investigator and prosecutor apart. Amit made it a mid-episode recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a magnificent and very libertarian book. He was delighted that Ajay, whom he teases as a 'secret statist', cited it.

recommendations.item: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay presents this episode as the second grand idea of dispersing power, after the earlier episode on decentralisation.
recommendations.reason: It is the companion piece. It covers spreading power downward across union, state and city governments under the subsidiarity principle, while this episode covers splitting power across the three branches.

recommendations.item: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist (Episode 88, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit points back to it while warning against judging the Constitution's framers with hindsight.
recommendations.reason: It covers Nehru's First Amendment as a mistake that should be understood in context. It also explains Amit's view that the Indian Constitution doesn't really protect free speech.

recommendations.item: The Anti-Defection Law (Episode 13, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining how the anti-defection law ended debate in Parliament.
recommendations.reason: A deeper look at how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that follow the whip.

recommendations.item: Our Parliament and Our Democracy (Episode 253, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
recommendations.context: The second of the two episodes Amit cites on the anti-defection law and Parliament's decline.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with MR Madhavan, whom both hosts admire. He talks at length about how the anti-defection law changed Parliament.

recommendations.item: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Episode 402, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recommended after Ajay mentions SEBI's founders imagining the institution and drafting the first SEBI Act.
recommendations.reason: This ten-and-a-half-hour conversation tells the inspiring story of SEBI's founding in great detail. Amit urges listeners to watch it.

recommendations.context: Ajay recalls that last year's conference, which Amit attended, had an entire session on recent developments in the US administrative state.
recommendations.reason: He calls the field red hot, full of interesting developments and good intellectual debates.

recommendations.context: A slim 1946 US law, pushed by Republicans uneasy about the expansion of government under Roosevelt.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'a phenomenal piece of work' and a blueprint for checks and balances in government agencies. A single rulebook binds every federal agency, which is the same idea behind India's draft Indian Financial Code. He cautions that you have to read it together with the court rulings that followed.

recommendations.item: XKDR Forum's paper on Indian courts
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: Cited as quantitative evidence that the Bombay and Delhi High Courts are now reasonably effective and efficient.
recommendations.reason: It weakens the 1992 argument for giving SEBI its own in-house judging. Ajay suggests the trade-offs have changed and the arrangement should be rethought.

recommendations.creator: Manam Chocolate
recommendations.context: The first of his promised recommendations, 'for some fun and silliness.'
recommendations.reason: A Hyderabad company making expensive, really good chocolate. Not sponsored, just something they love.

recommendations.creator: Andrew E Dessler
recommendations.reason: Ajay sees climate change as one of the great crises of the modern world, alongside populism. This slim, sensible book of about 200 pages covers climate science, mitigation and adaptation. He thinks everybody should read it.

recommendations.creator: IPCC
recommendations.context: A pick Ajay himself calls 'a little bit geeky.'
recommendations.reason: Ajay usually finds reports by international bodies such as the World Bank and IMF bland, because they are written by committee. IPCC reports are different. They are written by committees of scientists with real processes for debate, they give state-of-the-art thinking, and they show where experts disagree by setting out the range of models. He says just looking at the graphics will make you think about the world in new ways.

recommendations.creator: Ian Kershaw
recommendations.context: Ajay keeps thinking about the collapse of the Atlantic Alliance, which takes him back to 1940–41.
recommendations.reason: It shows how Churchill and Roosevelt worked to bring America into the Second World War on the Allied side. It was a close call: as late as August 1941, about half the House of Representatives still opposed it. Ajay finds it timely for understanding America today.

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: The first of three lesser-known Led Zeppelin songs.
recommendations.reason: Ajay thinks it is the greatest Led Zeppelin song that is not widely known.

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: An obscure Led Zeppelin track. Ajay challenges the crew to read the lyrics first.
recommendations.reason: Years ago he came across the lyrics before hearing it and wondered what kind of song they would make. The actual song is surprising and brilliant, and 'it'll just make you think about songs.'

recommendations.creator: Led Zeppelin
recommendations.context: From In Through the Out Door, the last Led Zeppelin album. John Bonham died shortly after it.
recommendations.reason: Ajay considers it one of the great things Plant, Page, John Paul Jones and Bonzo ever did, made at the peak of their powers just before the band ended.

core_ideas.explanation: This is Ajay's personal version of separation of powers. The Planner sits down and sets priorities, probabilities and a calendar. Then the Doer takes over and simply executes, without re-planning or worrying about the fifty other demands on his time. You trust the choice you already made, give the one task everything, and accept missing other deadlines. When the task is done, the Doer is kicked out and the Planner decides what comes next.
core_ideas.quote: That we get the full pleasure of doing one thing at a time well.

core_ideas.concept: Democracy is dispersion of power, not voting
core_ideas.explanation: Elections only choose who plays the legislative role. If voting just picked a king, he would be almost impossible to remove, because how could anyone organise an opposition against a king? Democracy really means checks and balances. One way to spread power is decentralisation: under the subsidiarity principle, each function goes to the lowest level of government that can handle it. The other is separation of powers.
core_ideas.quote: The essence of democracy is not elections. It is in checks and balances. It is in dispersion of power.

core_ideas.concept: Separation of powers, explained through a speech crime
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay uses a speech offence under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) to show how the three branches work. The legislature alone decides whether something, say defamation or sedition, is a crime, and it has to win elections to earn that power. The police only investigate against the written law and file a charge sheet. They cannot decide what is offensive or who deserves punishment. The judge alone decides on punishment after hearing both sides, and cannot go after anyone on her own initiative. Ajay calls this a mind-blowing achievement in political philosophy. He admits that as an economist, trained to treat government as one big monolith, it took him years to see how important it is.
core_ideas.quote: That's what only legislators can do. To write a law, you gotta win elections.

core_ideas.concept: The state should be a game of conflict
core_ideas.explanation: The three branches are meant to be co-equal, unafraid of each other, and in constant tension. Amit adds that friction, normally seen as bad, is good when it comes to the state. A slow process guards against hasty action. A formal separation also makes any power grab visible: Indira Gandhi's Emergency could not pass as normal democracy.
core_ideas.quote: This is not a happy family. This is not a harmonious family. It's a game of conflict.

core_ideas.concept: The fear test for arbitrary power
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay offers a simple test of whether checks and balances are working: is anyone in your country someone you are afraid of? Turning that ideal into practice takes concrete design: decentralisation, separate branches, and an investigator and prosecutor who are separate people and argue with each other. Borrowing David Friedman's phrase, this is 'the machinery of freedom.'
core_ideas.quote: You and me as the people should never be scared of a person. If you're scared of somebody, there's something wrong in your country because that somebody has arbitrary power.

core_ideas.explanation: This is an American term that Ajay recommends, partly because it opens the door to a large body of writing on the subject. The trend began with FDR's expansion of government. Ajay says no country has it worse than India: joint secretaries write the laws, district collectors double as district magistrates (a British legacy from when courts were scarce), and civil servants routinely play judge. Its Indian roots are a Constitution with no real separation of powers, the anti-defection law, and the peculiar way Indian parties work.
core_ideas.quote: The administrative state is a world where officials of the executive branch disproportionately exert legislative and judicial powers.

core_ideas.concept: The anti-defection law: good intentions, bad outcome
core_ideas.explanation: The anti-defection law of the late 1980s was meant to stop MPs switching sides for favours. Instead it forced every MP to vote as the party whip says, which ended genuine debate. MPs stopped reading bills, the bureaucracy ended up drafting the laws, and power within parties had already been centralised under Indira Gandhi. Together, these let the ruling party run both the executive and the legislature from the top.
core_ideas.quote: Now the idea of the anti-defection bill is awesome, but economists know: don't look at intention, look at outcome.

core_ideas.concept: Rules and norms: both matter, but only rules survive pressure
core_ideas.explanation: Every society runs on a mix of formal rules and informal norms. James Buchanan's public choice view is that lines written into law and the Constitution change incentives in a lasting way. Norms, like the standing-committee practice, can be swept away quickly. Yet norms still do real work. A judge who writes a bad ruling loses standing among her peers.
core_ideas.quote: These things have to be coded in rules. If it's in documents, if it's in the Constitution, then it's real.

core_ideas.concept: Separation of powers entered India through the basic structure doctrine
core_ideas.explanation: The Supreme Court built a core of the Constitution that Parliament cannot amend. It reasoned that Parliament is not a constituent assembly and is more open to majority impulses. The doctrine then grew in two ways. First, it became a test for all new laws, not just constitutional amendments. Second, it kept expanding as courts reread rights such as the right to life. Separation of powers came in this way. A plain reading of the text, or an LLM fed the Constitution, would say it isn't there. That is why Ajay is optimistic.
core_ideas.quote: So this is the way in which there is a separation of powers doctrine lurking inside the living constitution of India today. It came in through the basic structure.

core_ideas.explanation: A regulator that drafts rules, investigates, prosecutes and adjudicates combines all three branches. Parliament may hand narrow law-making power to officials, but it must be tightly controlled; doing too much of it is called 'excessive delegation.' The clean design is that the regulator investigates and decides whether to prosecute, and a real court or tribunal judges.
core_ideas.quote: Regulations are laws. So here you have unelected officials who are drafting law and that should like straight away make you a little squeamish

core_ideas.explanation: The US Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 applies the same rules on transparency and checks and balances to all federal agencies. India's draft Indian Financial Code, which Ajay worked on, took the same approach: about 140 sections governing every financial agency, whether RBI, SEBI or a debt management agency. The idea is that these basic rules of good conduct should not change depending on what an agency regulates.
core_ideas.quote: It is one single law that applies to all federal agencies.

core_ideas.concept: Who checks the judges? Their peers
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay cites Tarunabh Khaitan, a law academic in the UK: ministers, bureaucrats and parliamentarians should not have power over judges. The real check is reputation, meaning the respect of other judges, lawyers, law bloggers and academic journals. This makes a strong legal culture of critique a pillar of the rule of law.
core_ideas.quote: All of us, we are human. The currency we work for is the respect of our peers.

core_ideas.concept: Atrophy is the default; every generation must fight again
core_ideas.explanation: Amit worries that, given human nature and power, well-designed systems tend to decay. A party in power for long enough can fill every institution with its own people. Hence 'eternal vigilance', in words attributed to Jefferson. Ajay agrees that freedom has to be re-earned. He cites Angela Merkel saying Germany's true soul will be known only when the last people who lived through the Second World War have died, and notes that 20% of Germans now vote for the AfD.
core_ideas.quote: Just because your parents built a great country, you don't get a great country.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit cautions against treating any constitution, including the deeply flawed Indian one, like a holy book. A constitution is shaped by the circumstances in which it was written, and good design on paper is only the start. He quotes Andrew Breitbart's line that politics is downstream of culture. Liberty lasts only when citizens instinctively object every time freedom is infringed. Ajay agrees that in India the instinct is still to look for a strongman.
core_ideas.quote: the task of governance and designing a system is not done when you write a constitution. The task is done when those values percolate through society.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on Ajay's planner-doer framework: 'Amit the planner rocks… but Amit the doer is a frickin' nikamma.' Then he adds a third self: 'there's Amit the regretter… I could have been a contender.'
Ajay on absolute monarchy: 'If Aurangzeb said that off with his head, then Mr. Beer Biceps would have no choice.'
Ajay's dry jab at strongman worship: Rome's republic, the world's first, 'was destroyed by the great man Julius Caesar.'

Ajay on how economists picture government: 'you don't have some Aurangzeb and you're supposed to go whisper in Aurangzeb's ears that dude, we should do inflation targeting.' Amit promises viewers an on-screen cartoon of exactly that: 'What even are these images you are putting in my head?'

Amit, overjoyed that Ajay cited David Friedman: a very libertarian book 'which I did not expect from the secret statist… I've finally found a kindred soul.' Ajay replies: 'my heart sees the machinery of freedom, but my head has worked out all the compromises.'

Amit on what the anti-defection law did to Parliament: 'you could run parliament from an Excel sheet. You don't even need people to show up. Frankly, you don't even need to elect individual legislators.'
Before the chapter on regulators, Amit reminds Ajay 'explicitly for the camera' to be kind. Ajay's first verdict is that the original SEBI Act 'was just like a really bad piece of work.'

Amit predicts Perplexity would produce Ajay's whole basic-structure outline. Later, explaining the US Administrative Procedure Act, Ajay jabs back at 'the inability of perplexity to read one law and parse it' without the thousands of court rulings that interpret it.
Ajay on the climate change textbook: 'Nomsita will stay up at night with edge of the seat excitement around the Dessler book.'

Amit, after being promised six recommendations and getting seven ('a big bonus'), says Ajay's pitch for IPCC reports (a clutch of models, look at all the pictures, it will change how you see the world) applies equally to a teenager discovering the Sports Illustrated swimsuit edition. 'But you've been a different kind of teenager, I guess.'
Aristotle: Amit notes that Aristotle also described three branches of government, but as three functions of the state, not as a separation of powers.
Max Weber's definition of the state, via Ajay: 'a community that creates and maintains a monopoly of violence.'
The Pope crowning Napoleon: Ajay's example of kings allying with religion to claim absolute, divine authority.
Jefferson's 'alleged words' on eternal vigilance as the price of freedom, which Amit invokes against the slow decay of institutions.
Andrew Breitbart's 'politics is downstream of culture', which Amit uses to argue that the deeper battle for liberty is cultural.
Led Zeppelin: Robert Plant, Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones and 'Bonzo' at their peak on In Through the Out Door, the last album before John Bonham died and the band broke up.
